field_name: Multi-hop Knowledge Graph Question Answering with Language Models

categories.name: Language Model + Knowledge Graph Embedding
categories.description: Approaches that combine pretrained language models for question understanding with knowledge graph embeddings for entity/relation representation.

categories.name: Explicit-Implicit Relational Chain Reasoning
categories.description: Methods that simultaneously leverage explicit relational chains from questions and implicit chains from knowledge graphs.

categories.name: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
categories.description: Frameworks that retrieve relevant knowledge graph subgraphs or passages to augment language model generation for question answering.

categories.name: Dual-Graph Hybrid Retrieval
categories.description: RAG systems that model both linguistic relationships and document structure for improved retrieval.

categories.name: Graph-based Retrieval with Relation Embeddings
categories.description: Methods that construct document-level knowledge graphs and use vector embeddings of graph relations for retrieval.

categories.name: Question Decomposition
categories.description: Approaches that break down complex multi-hop questions into simpler semantic components for easier processing.

categories.name: Reasoning Network Architectures
categories.description: Custom neural network designs specifically engineered for multi-hop reasoning over knowledge graphs.

categories.name: Unrestricted Multi-hop Reasoning Network
categories.description: Network designs that avoid restrictive neighborhood constraints for more flexible reasoning paths.

categories.name: Logic-adaptive Multi-source Reasoning Fusion
categories.description: Methods that fuse reasoning from multiple sources with adaptive logic mechanisms.

categories.name: Graph Convolutional Network-based Relation Classification
categories.description: Approaches that use GCNs to improve relation classification for multi-hop KGQA.

categories.name: Progressive Planning and Reinforced Reasoning
categories.description: Frameworks that combine progressive planning strategies with reinforcement learning for LLM-guided reasoning.

idea_position: Local Context Subgraph Enrichment with Adaptive Repair Loop
common_assumptions: Language models can effectively encode natural language questions for KGQA tasks.
Knowledge graph embeddings capture semantic relations and can help overcome KG incompleteness.
Combining multiple sources of information (e.g., explicit and implicit chains, linguistic and structural features) improves reasoning performance.
Effective multi-hop QA requires modeling chains or paths of relations in the knowledge graph.
common_benchmarks: Custom domain-specific datasets (e.g., biomedical, construction safety)

repeated_limitations.description: Limited generalizability across different domains, datasets, or knowledge graph constructions.
Dependence on the quality, completeness, and accuracy of the underlying knowledge graph.
Computational complexity and memory constraints when reasoning over large knowledge graphs.
Limited explicit interpretability of the reasoning process in some neural approaches.
Challenges in handling noisy, conflicting, or missing information in knowledge graphs.

underexplored_combinations: Enriching training triples with local context subgraphs from the same source passage
Adaptive repair loops that detect and correct one-hop failures in KGQA
Combining local context enrichment with reinforcement learning optimization
Transfer learning from lower-hop to higher-hop QA via RL-based optimization
Integrating context subgraph enrichment with explicit-implicit relational chain reasoning

contradictions.description: Disagreement on the effectiveness of neighborhood constraints: some methods restrict reasoning to local subgraphs for efficiency (e.g., GraftNet, PullNet), while others argue unrestricted reasoning is necessary for interpretability and completeness.
Varying claims about the necessity of explicit relational chain annotations: some works require them for supervision, while others aim to work without expensive labeling.
Different assumptions about what constitutes useful context: some focus on document-level graphs, others on passage-level subgraphs, and others on logical path construction.
